title: We have sinned
hookLine: the Yom Kippur confessions are in the plural: all of us together
last: WE HAVE NO KING BUT YOU.

cards: A packed room on Yom Kippur. Everyone is fasting. The whole congregation starts listing sins out loud.
We have been guilty. We have betrayed. We have stolen.
We have spoken slander. And with each word, everyone taps their chest with a fist. Here's the strange part.
The gentle old man in the next row has never stolen anything in his life. And he's saying it too. We have stolen.

teach.b: Ashamnu means we have been guilty.
It's the first word of the short confession, and the list runs through the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav, one or two words per letter.
We have been guilty, we have betrayed, we have robbed, we have spoken slander, and on to the end.
The long confession that follows, Al Chet, is also alphabetical, and also in the plural: for the sin we have sinned before you. Every line is we. Why the alphabet?
People give different reasons. One is that we've sinned with every letter, every part of speech and life. Another is that the alphabet sets a limit.
The confession has an ending. You name it, and you stop. Why the plural?

teach.h: ONE BODY: RESPONSIBLE FOR EACH OTHER.
teach.b: A teaching handed down in the name of the mystic Isaac Luria says that all Israel is like one body. If one hand does wrong, the whole body is part of it.
The Talmud puts it in one line: all Israel are responsible for one another. So the old man saying we have stolen isn't lying.
He's standing with the people who did, sharing the weight, and maybe admitting the ways a community lets wrongs happen. There's a model for this in the Torah.
On the Day of Atonement, the high priest laid his hands on the goat and, in the old Jewish translation, would "confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel."
Not his own list. Everyone's. The confession is said in each Amidah of Yom Kippur, and in many communities on ordinary weekdays too.
In a room full of people, nobody has to confess alone.

how: Ashamnu and Al Chet are said in every Amidah of Yom Kippur, and in the repetition by the congregation together, each person lightly striking the chest at each sin; many communities also say Ashamnu in weekday prayers.

games.q: you've never stolen anything. the congregation reaches the line we have stolen. what do you do?
o: stay silent; it isn't true of you.
say it with everyone, and tap your chest.
change it to they have stolen.
games.why: everyone says it together. the plural means sharing responsibility: all Israel are responsible for one another.

practice: Think of a wrong in your world that isn't only yours, something in your family, your workplace, your town, and say it quietly in the plural: we have ignored, we have been unkind.
If you like, tap your chest once, lightly, and feel the weight shared, not dropped.
